title: Elihu speaks from chapter 32 to chapter 37 — why does the Lord’s verdict name Job and three friends and not him?
summary: Elihu is first named at Job 32:2, angry with Job and with the three friends, and speaks through chapter 37. When the Lord gives his verdict he names Eliphaz and his “two friends” and Job. The verses quoted do not say whether Elihu spoke rightly, or why he is not named.
text: KJV Job 2:11 names those who came: “Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite” KJV Job 32:2: “Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God.” KJV 32:3: “Also against his three friends was his wrath kindled, because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job.” KJV 32:4: “Now Elihu had waited till Job had spoken, because they were elder than he.” After Elihu’s last words, KJV 38:1: “Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said,” KJV 38:2: “Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?” Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 38:1: Μετὰ δὲ τὸ παύσασθαι Ἐλιοὺν τῆς λέξεως, εἶπεν ὁ Κύριος τῷ Ἰὼβ διὰ λαίλαπος καὶ νεφῶν, [And after Elius had ceased from his speech, the Lord said to Job through whirlwind and clouds,] KJV 42:7: “And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.” KJV 42:9: “So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord commanded them” Fetched from https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB38.htm.
reasoning: The narrator says Elihu was angry with both sides. Elihu is introduced as speaker at 32:6, 34:1 and 35:1 and again at 36:1, and a search of the packaged KJV of chapters 32–37 for a line that introduces a speaker (“answered … and said”, “spake … and said”, “proceeded, and said”) finds those four verses only. The Lord’s verdict at 42:7 sorts the speakers into those who did not speak rightly (Eliphaz and his two friends) and Job. Elihu is in neither group as named. Whether his speeches are approved, condemned or passed over changes how chapters 32–37 are to be read: as a true answer to Job, as one more mistaken speech, or as something the verdict does not address.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that Elihu is not rebuked because he spoke rightly; that the question at 38:2 is aimed at Elihu, the last to have spoken; that 38:2 is aimed at Job, as 38:1 says the Lord “answered Job”, and Elihu is simply passed over; and that the “two friends” of 42:7 are counted without him because he was not one of the three who came at 2:11. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV or in the Greek quoted, and this record asserts none. The Greek of 38:1 names Elihu as having ceased speaking, which the KJV verse does not, but it too says the Lord spoke “to Job”. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV of Job was searched for the name “Elihu”; it stands at 32:2, 32:4, 32:5, 32:6, 34:1, 35:1 and 36:1 and nowhere after chapter 36. That is a word search of one book, not a reading of the whole Bible, and Elihu’s speeches were not read in full for this record. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: “Ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath” — which words of Job are meant?
summary: The Lord tells Eliphaz that Job has spoken of him what is right. Shortly before, the Lord has asked who darkens counsel by words without knowledge and whether Job will condemn him, and Job has said that he uttered what he did not understand. The verse does not say which of Job’s words were right.
text: KJV Job 42:7: “And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.” KJV 42:8 repeats it: “in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job” The Lord to Job. KJV 38:2: “Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?” KJV 40:2: “Shall he that contendeth with the Almighty instruct him? he that reproveth God, let him answer it.” KJV 40:8: “Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?” Job to the Lord. KJV 40:4: “Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.” KJV 42:3: “Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not.” KJV 42:6: “Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.” Fetched from .
reasoning: Within five chapters the Lord both challenges Job’s words (38:2, 40:2, 40:8) and holds up Job’s speech as right against the friends’ (42:7, 42:8), and Job himself says that he uttered what he did not understand (42:3) and that he repents (42:6). The verdict names no speech. Which words it approves decides how Job’s long complaints in the dialogue are to be read: as right speech about God, or as the words without knowledge that the Lord challenged.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that the right words are Job’s last answers (40:4–5 and 42:2–6); that they are his speeches as a whole, set against what the friends said of God; and that the verdict is about speaking to the Lord and not about what was said of him. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, and this record asserts none. The two sets of verses need not conflict: a speaker can be right in one thing and without knowledge in another, and the passage does not say that this is how they fit. A separate record compares the Greek of 42:7–9; the Greek of 42:7 quoted there has “as my servant Job” and names no speech either, and the Greek of 42:8 is worded differently. A published record on 42:7 notes that the book corrects its own speakers; it does not ask which of Job’s words are approved. Check made: Job 38:1–3, 40:1–8 and 42:1–9 were read in the packaged KJV; Job’s speeches in chapters 3–31 were not re-read for this record, and no other book was searched. title: Behemoth and leviathan — what creatures does the Lord point Job to?
summary: The Lord’s speech from the whirlwind (40:6) sets two creatures before Job, behemoth and leviathan, and describes each at length. The KJV keeps both words as names. The verses quoted do not say what kind of creature either one is.
text: KJV Job 40:15: “Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox.” KJV 40:17: “He moveth his tail like a cedar” KJV 40:23: “Behold, he drinketh up a river, and hasteth not” KJV Job 41:1: “Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook? or his tongue with a cord which thou lettest down?” KJV 41:19: “Out of his mouth go burning lamps, and sparks of fire leap out.” KJV 41:21: “His breath kindleth coals, and a flame goeth out of his mouth.” KJV 41:34: “He beholdeth all high things: he is a king over all the children of pride.” The name leviathan elsewhere in the KJV. Psalms 74:14: “Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces” Psalms 104:26: “There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein.” Isaiah 27:1: “shall punish leviathan the piercing serpent, even leviathan that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea” Hebrew (WLC) 40:15: הִנֵּה־נָ֣א בְ֭הֵמֹות. Hebrew (WLC) for KJV 41:1, numbered 40:25 in that edition: תִּמְשֹׁ֣ךְ לִוְיָתָ֣ן בְּחַכָּ֑ה. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/40/.
reasoning: The speech uses the two creatures to answer Job, so what they are bears on what the answer is. The description joins things said of a grazing animal and a creature of the water (grass, a river, a hook) with things that go beyond that (a flame from the mouth, heads in the plural in the psalm, a kingship over “all the children of pride”). If they are animals Job could see, the speech points to God’s rule over the made world; if they are creatures of another kind, it points to powers beyond it. The text names them and does not say which.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that they are two known animals described in heightened language; that they are animals no longer known; and that they are creatures of a kind other than ordinary animals, as Isaiah 27:1 speaks of leviathan beside “the dragon that is in the sea”. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV or in the Hebrew quoted, and this record asserts none. The speech is in verse, and this record does not test its pictures against natural history. A shared name in the Psalms and Isaiah does not settle that the same creature is meant in Job. Two separate records compare the Greek, which has “beasts” at 40:15 and a common noun for a dragon or serpent at KJV 41:1; the Greek verses quoted in those records keep neither name. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for the words “behemoth” (Job 40:15 only) and “leviathan” (Job 41:1, Psalms 74:14, Psalms 104:26, Isaiah 27:1), and those verses were read. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and Job 40:15–41:34 was not compared with the Hebrew or the Greek verse by verse. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original.
